title: Ša naqba īmuru
source: Epic of Gilgameš, Standard Babylonian version, Tablet I 1–8 (ed. A. R. George 2003; eBL edition, SB I)
about: The epic opens by praising Gilgameš, king of Uruk, for the wisdom he won on his travels. This is Standard Babylonian, the later literary dialect, not Old Babylonian: the final -m has gone, so māti, not mātim.

badge.name: He Who Saw the Deep
badge.about: Read the opening lines of the Epic of Gilgameš

lines.en: He who saw the Deep, the foundation of the land,

q.prompt: What had the hero seen?
options: the Deep, the foundation of the land
the face of the sun god

lines.en: who knew all the ways, was wise in everything!

lines.t: Gilgāmeš ša naqba īmuru išdī māti,
lines.g: 𒀭𒄑𒂆𒈦 𒃻 𒅘𒁀 𒄿𒈬𒊒 𒅖𒁲 𒈠𒀀𒋾
lines.en: Gilgameš, who saw the Deep, the foundation of the land,

q.prompt: Who is the man who saw the Deep?

lines.en: who knew all the ways, was wise in everything!
He explored the seats of power everywhere,
he knew the sum of wisdom about all things.

q.prompt: What did he come to know?
options: the sum of wisdom about all things
the names of all the gods

lines.en: He saw the secret and uncovered the hidden;
he brought back word from before the Flood.

q.prompt: What did he bring back?

title: Šumma awīlum īn mār awīlim
source: Laws of Hammurabi §§ 196–198, 200, stele Louvre Sb 8, rev. xvii 45–59, 66–70 (CDLI P249253), c. 1750 BC (trimmed)
about: Hammurabi's laws punish an injury with the same injury, but only between equals. Hurting a muškēnum, a commoner, costs silver instead.

badge.name: Hammurabi's Clerk
badge.about: Read the eye-for-an-eye laws on Hammurabi's stele

lines.t: šumma awīlum īn mār awīlim uḫtappid,
lines.g: 𒋳𒈠 𒀀𒉿𒈝 𒄿𒅔 𒌉 𒀀𒉿𒅆 𒌔𒋰𒁉𒀉
lines.en: If a man blinds the eye of another free man,
they shall blind his eye.

q.prompt: What happens to a man who blinds a free man's eye?
options: he pays a mina of silver

lines.en: If he breaks a free man's bone,
they shall break his bone.

q.prompt: What is the rule behind these first two laws?
options: the attacker suffers the same injury
the attacker pays the victim's family
the judges decide each case freely

lines.t: šumma īn muškēnim uḫtappid u lū eṣemti muškēnim ištebir,
lines.g: 𒋳𒈠 𒄿𒅔 𒈦𒂗𒆕 𒌔𒋰𒁉𒀉 𒅇 𒇻 𒄊𒉻𒁺 𒈦𒂗𒆕 𒅖𒋼𒁉𒅕
lines.en: If he blinds a commoner's eye or breaks a commoner's bone,
he shall pay one mina of silver.

q.prompt: What is the penalty for injuring a commoner?
options: a fine of one mina of silver

lines.t: šumma awīlum šinni awīlim meḫrišu ittadi,
lines.g: 𒋳𒈠 𒀀𒉿𒈝 𒅆𒅔𒉌 𒀀𒉿𒅆 𒈨𒄴𒊑𒋗 𒀉𒋫𒁲
lines.en: If a man knocks out the tooth of a man who is his equal,
they shall knock out his tooth.

q.prompt: Why does this law say 'his equal'?
options: a tooth for a tooth applies only between equals

title: Ana Zinû qibīma
source: Letter of Iddin-Sîn to his mother Zinû, from Larsa, Louvre AO 8372 (TCL 18 111 = AbB 14 165; CDLI P387407), Old Babylonian (trimmed)
about: A young man writes home to complain that other boys get finer clothes than he does, even the son of his father's employee, a boy whose mother had adopted him. It is the most famous family letter to survive from Babylonia.

badge.name: Dear Mother
badge.about: Read a son's complaining letter home

lines.en: Say to Zinû:
thus says Iddin-Sîn:

q.prompt: Who is writing to whom?

lines.t: Šamaš Marduk u Ilabrat aššumīya ana dāriātim liballiṭūki.
lines.g: 𒀭𒌓 𒀭𒀫𒌓 𒅇 𒀭𒎏𒋚 𒀸𒋳𒅀 𒀀𒈾 𒁕𒊑𒀀𒁴 𒇷𒁀𒀠𒇷𒁺𒆠
lines.en: May Šamaš, Marduk and Ilabrat keep you well forever for my sake.

lines.t: ṣubāt awīlê šattam ana šattim idammiqū,
lines.g: 𒌆𒍪𒁀𒀀𒀜 𒀀𒉿𒇷𒂊 𒊭𒀜𒌓 𒀀𒈾 𒊭𒀜𒁴 𒄿𒁕𒄠𒈪𒆪
lines.en: The gentlemen's clothes get better year after year,

lines.t: atti ṣubātī šattam ana šattim tuqallalī.
lines.g: 𒀜𒋾 𒌆𒍪𒁀𒀀𒋾 𒊭𒀜𒌓 𒀀𒈾 𒊭𒀜𒁴 𒌅𒂵𒀠𒆷𒇷

lines.en: While you gave birth to me,
his mother adopted him;

you do not love me.

title: Inūma ilū awīlum
source: Atrahasis, Old Babylonian version, Tablet I 1–8, 12–13, from the Sippar copy BM 78941 (ed. W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard 1969; eBL edition, OB I) (trimmed)
about: The Babylonian flood story begins before people existed, when the junior gods, the Igigi, had to do all the hard work. Their revolt will lead to the creation of mankind, and later to the Flood. This is Old Babylonian, copied in the 17th century BC.

badge.name: When the Gods Were Men

title: Kikkiš kikkiš igār igār
source: Epic of Gilgameš, Standard Babylonian version, Tablet XI 21–25, 27–28, 30–31 (ed. A. R. George 2003; eBL edition, SB XI); cuneiform after the Babylon copy BM 35380, and the Nineveh copy K 8517 for part of line 24 and lines 28–31 (trimmed)
about: Ūta-napišti tells Gilgameš how he survived the Flood. The gods had sworn to keep their plan secret, so the god Ea spoke to the reed wall of Ūta-napišti's house, knowing he would hear. This is Standard Babylonian, from tablets of the first millennium BC, not Old Babylonian.
